title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Avery Chen
summary: Company-wide architecture and engineering standards that unify API, coding, infra, model-serving, observability, and performance requirements, plus canonical ADRs for recent major decisions.
body:
Overview:

This doc consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model serving, observability, and performance. It also collects key ADRs (Architecture Decision Records) affecting these areas. The goal is to reduce cognitive load for engineers, ensure interoperable subsystems, and make trade-offs explicit and discoverable.

Sections included:
- API Standards
- Coding Standards
- Infrastructure (IaC) Standards
- Model-Serving Standards
- Observability Standards
- Performance Standards and SLOs
- Canonical ADRs (summaries)
- Enforcement, ownership, and review process

1) API Standards

Purpose: APIs are the contract between services, SDKs, and customers. They must be stable, discoverable, and testable.

Core rules:
- OpenAPI-first: All public and internal HTTP services MUST publish an OpenAPI v3 spec in the repo root at openapi.yaml. The spec is the source of truth for SDK generation and contract testing.
- Versioning: Use semantic versioning for API surfaces. Major version bumps (breaking changes) require an ADR and a documented migration guide. Prefer path-based versioning (/v1/...).
- Backwards compatibility: Additive changes are OK; deletions or reshaping responses are breaking. When adding fields, mark experimental fields with x-experimental:true in the OpenAPI extension.
- Idempotency: POST endpoints that create resources must accept an Idempotency-Key header and guarantee at-least-once semantics are handled correctly.
- Error model: Responses MUST follow the standard error envelope: {"error": {"code": string, "message": string, "details": optional }}. Map common error codes: invalid_request (400), unauthorized (401), not_found (404), rate_limited (429), server_error (500).
- Pagination: Cursor-based pagination is required for list endpoints that can return >100 items. Use standardized query params: page_size, page_token.
- Throttling headers: All services MUST return X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset when rate-limited.
- Contract tests: Each service MUST include contract tests that validate the OpenAPI spec against a running instance. CI must run these tests on PR.
- SDK compatibility: Backwards-compatible changes should not break generated SDKs. When changing response shapes, version the OpenAPI and release SDKs through the monorepo pipeline.

API security:
- All internal services use mTLS. Public-facing endpoints use OAuth2 or API keys with least privilege. Secrets must never appear in logs.

API Example (required headers table):
| Header | Required | Description |
|--------|----------|-------------|
| Authorization | yes | Bearer token or API key |
| Content-Type | yes | application/json or application/x-ndjson for streaming |
| Idempotency-Key | conditional | Required for create endpoints when clients retry |
| X-Request-ID | recommended | For tracing across services |

2) Coding Standards

Purpose: Maintainable, secure, and performant code across services.

Languages and runtimes:
- Primary backend languages: Go (latency-sensitive services), Python (data/ETL, evals), TypeScript (frontend and some infra tooling). New services should justify other runtimes in an ADR.

Formatting and linting:
- Enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff/isort for Python, and ESLint/Prettier for TypeScript.
- CI enforces linters and formatters; PRs failing linters are blocked.

Testing:
- Unit tests: target >= 80% coverage on critical modules.
- Integration tests: each service must have a small suite that can run in CI (service mocks or docker-compose).
- End-to-end: critical flows (deploy -> smoke -> rollback) must be covered by the platform test harness.

PR guidelines:
1. Keep changes < 400 lines where possible. 2. Describe the intent, impact, and rollout plan in the PR. 3. Assign an approver from the owning service. 4. Add a changelog entry for public or SDK-impacting changes.

Dependency management:
- Use curated dependency policy: patch upgrades automatically, feature upgrades require PR and CI validation.
- No direct commits to main for dependency bumps; use automated PRs from the dependency bot.

3) Infrastructure (IaC) Standards

Purpose: Reliable, auditable, and repeatable provisioning of cloud resources.

Terraform:
- All cloud infra must be declared in Terraform modules under infra/ in the monorepo. Modules must be reusable and documented.
- State backend: use remote state (Terraform Cloud or S3+Dynamo for locking).
- Environments: dev/staging/prod must be separate workspaces and follow the same module interfaces.

Tagging and naming:
- All resources require tags: team, project, environment, cost_center. Naming conventions must use the pattern: rdx-{team}-{service}-{env}-{resource}.

Networking:
- VPCs must follow the standardized subnets and allowlist model. No public subnets for model-gpu clusters in production without explicit security review.

Secrets and keys:
- Use KMS/HSM for root keys and store application secrets in secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager). Keys rotated annually or on suspected compromise.

Capacity & autoscaling:
- Define target utilization for services (CPU/GPU/Memory). For GPU pools, maintain 70% target utilization and >10% spare capacity buffer for burst requests.

4) Model-Serving Standards

Purpose: Ensure predictable, cost-effective, and safe inference serving across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Model lifecycle:
- Model registry: All production models must be registered with metadata: model_id, version, quantization_profile, supported_seq_lengths, owner, eval_scorecards.
- Versioning: Models are versioned semantically. Backwards-incompatible tokenizer/model changes require a compatibility test suite.

Quantization and kernels:
- Quantization profiles must be checked into quantization-profiles/ with performance and quality delta measurements. Each profile must include a recommended kernel set.

Routing and fallbacks:
- Smart routing rules: requests may be routed by latency target, cost budget, or region. Policy is defined in route configs with priorities.
- Fallbacks: every public route must declare at least one fallback model variant and a fallback region. Fallback behavior must preserve API contract.

Caching and batching:
- Implement prefix caching and KV-cache reuse per model where applicable. Batching config must expose max_batch_size and max_batch_latency.

Safety and content filters:
- All externally-facing models must run the safety filter pipeline. Filter thresholds and escalation flow are maintained in quality-guardrails/.

Runbooks and canaries:
- Deployments require a canary rollout (min 5% traffic) with automated metrics checks (latency, error rate, quality score on golden prompts) before full rollout.

5) Observability Standards

Purpose: Fast detection and diagnosis of issues; provide SLO-driven alerts to reduce alert fatigue.

Instrumentation:
- Use OpenTelemetry for traces and standardized metrics instrumentation libraries for Go and Python.
- Metrics naming convention: rdx.<service>.<metric_name>.<unit> (e.g. rdx.inference.latency_ms.p95).

Standard metrics to emit:
- request.count (per-route)
- request.error_count (per-route, by error code)
- latency_ms.p50/p95/p99 (per-route, token ranges)
- tokens.generated.count
- batch.size.avg
- gpu.utilization and gpu.memory.free

Tracing and logs:
- All public-facing requests must carry a trace (X-Request-ID linked to trace id).
- Logs must be structured JSON with keys: ts, level, service, request_id, user_id (if applicable), msg, err.

Dashboards and alerts:
- Dashboards: per-route latency, error rate, token cost, and quality regressions.
- Alerting policy: Alerts should target sympoms of SLO breach. Only actionable alerts with runbook links are allowed.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs

Purpose: Define measurable targets for latency, availability, and quality to guide engineering tradeoffs.

Platform SLOs (examples):
- Hosted API availability: 99.95% monthly uptime for api.redwood.com (excludes planned maintenance).
- Latency (generation endpoints): For standard workload (<=128 tokens): p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 1s. For <=512 tokens: p95 <= 600ms, p99 <= 2.5s.
- Disabled/Throttle fallback: If latency SLO cannot be maintained, platform must automatically route to lower-cost/latency model variant and tag response with X-Fallback-Model.
- Error budget policy: Product teams consume error budget; SRE will propose remediation once 25% of monthly error budget is consumed.

Cost-performance guidelines:
- Target per-token cost reduction levers: batching (target 30-50% cost reduction when batching 8-32 requests), quantization (apply Q4_8 when acceptable quality delta < 1 BLEU/metric point), and caching.

Benchmarking:
- All model onboarding must include a perf-suite run with: seq lengths [64,128,256,512], batch sizes [1,4,8,16], and collect p50/p95/p99 latencies and tokens/sec. Results are stored in benchmarking-and-perf-suite/.

7) Canonical ADRs (summaries)

ADR-001: Unified model variant naming (2024-06-18)
- Decision: Adopt stable naming scheme: {model_family}-{size}-{precision}-{variant} (e.g. redwood-rlhf-7b-q4_8-fast).
- Rationale: Simplifies routing, caching keys, and model discovery.
- Consequences: Tooling updated to parse names; old names supported via aliasing layer for 6 months.

ADR-012: Primary runtime language for latency-critical services (2025-02-02)
- Decision: Go is the primary language for latency-sensitive runtime services (serving gateway, request router). Python remains primary for evals and offline tooling.
- Rationale: better perf characteristics, static binary delivery, simpler concurrency model.
- Consequences: New teams must demonstrate strong justification for other runtimes; some infra libraries reimplemented in Go.

ADR-021: Fallback-first routing policy (2025-08-12)
- Decision: When a primary model or region is degraded, route 100% of requests to a verified fallback variant instead of returning errors.
- Rationale: Improves availability and degrades gracefully.
- Consequences: Need to maintain and evaluate fallback variants for quality; additional cost for running fallbacks.

8) Enforcement, ownership, and review process

Ownership:
- Each standard area has an owning group:
  - API standards: eng-developer-experience
  - Coding standards: eng-platform
  - Infra standards: eng-infra
  - Model-serving standards: eng-serving-runtime + applied-ml-and-evals
  - Observability: eng-platform + eng-sre
  - Performance SLOs: eng-sre + product

Change process:
1. Propose changes as an ADR in the architecture-and-standards/adr/ directory.
2. Add reviewers from at least two affected teams.
3. Run a 7-day review window, gather feedback, and update the ADR.
4. Publish and schedule a rollout with tests and monitoring.

Audit and cadence:
- Standards are reviewed quarterly. Major changes must include migration guides and a deprecation timeline.

Appendix A: Example Terraform module usage:
```hcl
module "rdx_inference_cluster" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/terraform-modules.git//inference-cluster"
  team = "search"
  environment = "prod"
  gpu_instance_type = "a100-80gb"
  desired_capacity = 24
}
```

Appendix B: OpenAPI enforcement CI snippet (example):
```bash
# validate openapi spec and run contract tests
openapi-cli validate openapi.yaml
python -m contract_tests.run --spec openapi.yaml --target http://localhost:8080
```

Contact and feedback: For questions or requests to amend these standards, open a PR against this repo and ping the owning team.
